name: London System
family: 1.d4 with an early Bf4 (Queen's Pawn Game)
summary: The London System is a solid, low-theory 1.d4 system for White: the dark-squared bishop comes to f4 before e3, then White builds the c3-d4-e3 'triangle' with Nf3, Nbd2, Bd3 (or Be2 against a fianchetto), h3 when needed and O-O. Because the setup barely changes against 1...d5, 1...Nf6, 1...e6 or 1...g6, you can spend your time on plans instead of memorising moves: the Ne5 outpost, the e4 break, and a kingside attack with Qf3/Qh5 or Bxh7+ ideas. The modern move order 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 (or 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4) avoids some ...Qb6 problems of the old 2.Nf3 order, but you must know how to protect b2 once the bishop has left c1.
keyIdeas: Bishop out first: Bf4 before e3, so it is not locked behind the e-pawn as in the Colle System.
The pawn triangle c3-d4-e3: if Black takes on d4 we recapture with a pawn and keep the centre.
When Black offers a bishop trade with ...Bd6, step back with Bg3 (after ...Bxg3 hxg3 the h-file opens); against an early ...Bd6 before ...Nf6, Bxd6 followed by c4 is also good.
b2 is loose once the bishop leaves c1: answer ...Qb6 with Qb3 (a trade on b3 opens the a-file for us), Qc2 or Qc1, or with a well-timed Nc3/Nb5 that punishes ...Qxb2.
Ne5 is the London outpost: backed by d4 and the f4-bishop, it supports Qf3-h3, Qh5 or f4 kingside attacks.
The e4 break wins space and often threatens e5, forking pieces on d6 and f6; it is strongest after Black has played ...b6 or ...c4.
h3 gives the bishop the h2 retreat, so ...Nh5 or ...e5 does not win it; against ...g6 setups put the light-squared bishop on e2, not d3.
The Greek gift Bxh7+ only works when the f6-knight has gone, Ng5+ cannot simply be taken (...Bxg5/...Qxg5) and the queen can reach h5 quickly. Check it concretely: it fails more often than it works.
typicalPlans: Main structure (Black ...d5/...e6/...c5): c3, Nbd2, Bd3, O-O, then Ne5 with Qf3/Qh3, or the e4 break.
Against ...Qb6: Qb3; after ...Qxb3 axb3 use the half-open a-file, after ...c4 Qc2 prepare e4 to hit the over-extended c4-pawn.
Against King's Indian and fianchetto setups: h3, Be2, O-O, c3 or a4, keeping Bh2 ready for ...Nh5 or ...e5; meet a premature ...e5 with dxe5 and Nxe5.
In Carlsbad-type structures (after ...cxd4 exd4) play on the kingside and on e5 while Black tries the minority attack ...b5-b4.
Switch to c4 (Queen's Gambit play) when Black copies us with an early ...Bf5: b7 and d5 become targets.
commonMistakes: Playing e3 before Bf4 and burying the bishop.
Ignoring ...Qb6 and leaving b2 hanging, or answering with Qc1 while d4 is protected only by the queen (1.d4 c6 2.Bf4 Qb6 3.Qc1? Qxd4).
Bg5 against ...Nh5 when Black has NOT played ...e6: ...h6 and ...g5 chase the bishop. With ...e6 played, Bg5 is good because it hits the d8-queen.
Playing Bxh7+ by reflex: it fails when Black can answer Ng5+ with ...Bxg5 or ...Qxg5.
Putting the light-squared bishop on d3 against ...g6, where it bites on the g6-pawn.
Exchanging on c5 or d5 too early and releasing the central tension for nothing.

lines.name: Main line: ...e6, ...c5, ...Bd6 - Bg3 and the e4 break
lines.description: The classical main line: Black builds a Queen's Gambit Declined setup with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Bd6. We keep the bishop with Bg3, develop Bd3 and break with e4 as soon as Black loosens the long diagonal with ...b6. The same position arises from 2...e6 3.e3 Nf6, from 3...c5 4.Nf3 e6 and from 1...Nf6 2.Bf4 d5. Black's other choices on the way: 4...Bd6 (5.Bg3, or 5.Bxd6 as in the 2...e6 line); 4...Be7 (see the ...Be7 line); 4...Bd7 (planning ...Bb5) - keep the same setup and take on b5 if the bishops meet; 5...Bd6 or 5...Be7 instead of 5...Nc6 - same plans (Nbd2, Bg3/Bd3, Ne5); 5...Qb6 - 6.Qb3 as in the ...Qb6 line; 6...Be7 or 6...cxd4 7.exd4 - Bd3, O-O, Ne5 and Qe2/Qf3; 6...Nh5 - see the ...Nh5 line. Odd first moves such as 1...h6 or 1...a6, and 2...a6 after 1...d5, are met by the normal setup (Bf4, e3, Nf3, c3). Black's other 3rd moves: 3...g6 (see the 2...g6 line) and 3...Bd7 (4.Nf3, same setup). Quiet 4th, 5th and 6th moves such as 4...a6, 4...h6, 5...Bd7, 5...a6 or 6...h6 do not change the plan (Nbd2, Bd3, O-O, Ne5 or e4); 6...c4 is met by 7.b3 or 7.a4 and a later e4 break.

lines.name: Main line with 6...Nh5: 7.Bg5!

lines.name: ...Be7 setup: Ne5, Qf3 and the kingside attack
lines.description: If Black develops the bishop to e7, our f4-bishop is not challenged and we can attack with Ne5, Qf3-h3 and g4. lines.name: 2...e6 3.e3 Bd6: 4.Bxd6
lines.description: Black can challenge our bishop at once with ...Bd6 before developing the g8-knight. Here 4.Bxd6 is the most precise (4.Bg3, keeping the bishop as in the main line, is also fine). After 4...Qxd6 continue 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 with Rc1/Qb3 ideas. 3...Nf6 or 3...c5 transposes to the main line after 4.Nf3, and 3...Be7 4.Nf3 leads to the ...Be7 line. On move 5, 5...dxc4 6.Bxc4 Nf6 is similar to the line; 5...Qb6 6.Qb3 trades queens favourably; 5...Ne7 6.Nc3 and Nf3. Now 7.Qb3 c4 8.Qxb6 axb6 is comfortable for Black, so we hit back with 7.dxc5: 7...Qxc5 8.Nb3 gains time, and 7...Qxb2 8.Nd4 Ne4 9.Qc1 Qxc1+ 10.Rxc1 is a level endgame. (after ...Nxf4 exf4 Black's c-pawn is gone and we keep a lead), 6...Bg4 7.Qb3 (hitting b7), 6...c4 7.Ne5 or 7.b3.

lines.description: Against the early ...c5 and ...Nc6, 4.Nc3 is a Jobava-style alternative to 4.c3. The natural 4...Qb6?? (hitting b2) removes the only defender of d5. lines.name: 2...c5 3.e3 cxd4 4.exd4: Carlsbad structure
lines.description: Black exchanges on d4 early. After exd4 and c3 we get a Carlsbad structure with colours reversed (an Exchange Caro-Kann with an extra tempo for us): we play on the kingside and on e5, Black looks for the minority attack ...b5-b4. lines.name: King's Indian setup: ...Nbd7 and an early ...e5 (dxe5 and Nxe5)
